newsitem.title: USA: Families mourn ValuJet dead at memorial service.
newsitem.headline: Families mourn ValuJet dead at memorial service.

text.p: A bell tolled for the dead as their names were read, one by one.
At a memorial service on Sunday for the 110 people killed a year ago in the Everglades crash of ValuJet Inc's Flight 592, relatives struggled with grief and anger.

"The pain is still there, there is no closure," said Marguerite Dingle, who lost her sister Frances Brown in the crash, speaking to reporters after the ceremony. "The remains have not been found of my sister, there is no closure for us."
On May 11 last year, a fire erupted on the Atlanta-bound DC-9 jet shortly after takeoff from Miami International Airport.
The pilot radioed for help and tried to turn back, but the plane nose-dived into the Everglades, killing everyone aboard.
Preliminary reports indicated that the crash was caused by a fire in the cargo hold, ignited by oxygen generating canisters that had been mislabeled and improperly secured.
At an ecumenical religious service on Sunday -- Mother's Day in the United States -- ministers from various faiths sought to provide spiritual solace for those who lost their loved ones.

"God knows the pain...the burden...the grief you experienced," Rev. Freeman Wyche told relatives and friends of the dead at the First United Methodist Church in Miami's Coral Gables district. "He will see you through, no matter how cruel the cross, no matter how dark the valley."
Candles were lit for each of the victims of the tragedy; the church echoed with cries of grief and words of consolation in Creole, Hebrew, Spanish and English.
But at a news conference following the service, the relatives and friends voiced anger, saying the tragedy could have been prevented and that it could happen again.
They demanded action from the government to stop such a disaster from ever happening again.

"The ValuJet Flight 592 families are appalled at the present safety situation," said Laura Sawyer, the granddaughter of two of the victims. "Simply put, a year has passed and nothing has been done to make flying safer.

"We still haven't had fire detection and suppression systems in the cargo areas of planes; we still see hazardous materials being transported on a daily basis in commercial aircraft; and finally we still see the FAA value airline cost considerations over human lives," she said.
"All these factors must change."

As grim-faced relatives, some holding pictures of the dead, looked on in silence, others called for Atlanta-based ValuJet Inc to be closed down; others still said the government had not met its responsibilities.
Rev. Warren Lathem, who lost his son Ray in the crash, referred to the Federal Aviation Administration as "the tombstone agency."
"Nothing's happened...it would cost $125,000 more or less to put fire suppression and smoke detectors on each plane...which does not have them. That is a mild, mild amount of money."
ValuJet maintains that no decision or action by the airline or its employees can be linked to the accident.
The Miami Herald reported last week that the National Transportation Safety Board's final report on the crash, due in July, would censure the airline and the FAA.
NTSB officials declined to comment but said the board can only emit recommendations, not censure.
The FBI and a federal grand jury in Miami are still investigating the case, including allegations that federal documents may have been falsified.

The Herald also quoted chief NTSB investigator John Goglia as saying that everyone aboard the plane was dead before it hit the ground, something analysts had speculated but that the NTSB has not commented on publicly.
